Rewarding Doubt: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to
Confidence Calibration of Large Language Models
Paul Stangel * 1 David Bani-Harouni * 1 2 Chantal Pellegrini * 1 2 Ege Özsoy 1 2 Kamilia Zaripova 1 2
Matthias Keicher † 1 2 Nassir Navab † 1 2
Abstract
A safe and trustworthy use of Large Language
Models (LLMs) requires an accurate expression
of confidence in their answers. We introduce a
novel Reinforcement Learning (RL) approach for
LLM calibration that fine-tunes LLMs to elicit
calibrated confidence estimations in their answers
to factual questions. We model the problem as
a betting game where the model predicts a confidence score together with every answer, and
design a reward function that penalizes both over
and under-confidence. We prove that under our
reward design an optimal policy would result in
a perfectly calibrated confidence estimation. Our
experiments demonstrate significantly improved
confidence calibration and generalization to new
tasks without re-training, indicating that our approach teaches a general confidence awareness.
This approach enables the training of inherently
calibrated LLMs.
1. Introduction
In human intelligence and inter-human interaction, the ability to understand our own uncertainty and communicate
our doubts to others is fundamental for effective decisionmaking, collaboration, and learning (Cosmides & Tooby,
1996; Xiong et al., 2024). Similarly, for Large Language
Models (LLMs) to be safely used in real-world applications,
especially when humans and AI systems work together, they
must not only generate accurate information but also communicate their confidence in that information. While LLMs
have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding, question answering and text summa-

as their tendency to generate inaccurate information, often
referred to as hallucinations (Hadi et al., 2023). This raises
concerns about their reliability, particularly in real-world applications where trustworthiness is essential. Especially in
high-stakes environments such as medical diagnosis, where
LLMs are starting to become support tools for professionals
(Moor et al., 2023; Pellegrini et al., 2023; Tu et al., 2024;
Bani-Harouni et al., 2024), overconfident predictions including factual errors or hallucinations could have serious consequences for patient health. Also, in customer service or legal

to express uncertainty and defer complex queries to human
representatives when unsure to avoid misinformed decisions.
Reliable confidence estimation would enable these systems
to flag uncertain outputs for human review, ensuring that
crucial decisions are not made based on uncertain LLM outputs. To allow risk estimation while using LLM-generated
output, model confidence should be calibrated, meaning that
the expressed numerical confidence should be equal to the
probability of the model’s answer being correct.

et al., 2024). Additionally, this does not give models an
inherent awareness of confidence. Other trained methods
in this area generally do not explicitly optimize for calibration but instead for a binary correctness target (Azaria &
Mitchell, 2023; Kapoor et al., 2024). While this ensures
strong performance in terms of discrimination, it overlooks
the practical importance of fine-grained and well-calibrated
confidence scores. Without proper calibration, users cannot reliably interpret confidence values, making it difficult
to determine when to trust a model’s predictions. This is
particularly problematic in real-world applications where
decision thresholds vary based on context. For example, a
high-stakes clinical decision requires high confidence, while
a low-stakes trivia question might tolerate lower confidence.
By contrast, well-calibrated models enable more flexible
and trustworthy human interaction, allowing users to dynamically adjust their confidence requirements based on the
stakes of a given decision.

LLMs to express their calibrated confidence, encouraging a
granular, accurate estimation of the confidence level in the
training objective. For this, we model confidence estimation
as a betting game: a high-confidence answer would warrant
a larger bet, reflecting a strong belief in its correctness,
while a lower confidence score would suggest caution.
Our reward function is designed to reflect the risk-reward
tradeoff in betting, as illustrated in Figure 1. It increases the
reward when a correct answer is given with high confidence,
simulating the higher stakes of big bets. Conversely, it
penalizes incorrect answers more when they are made with
high confidence, discouraging overconfidence. This ensures
that both uncertainty and confidence are appropriately
factored into the reward system. With our reward design,
the model learns to align its predicted confidence with the
accuracy of its output, encouraging granular and calibrated
confidence scoring, as a calibrated confidence estimation
will provably result in the highest reward during training.
This not only improves the trustworthiness of LLMs in
collaborative human-AI scenarios but also helps users better
assess when AI tools should be trusted, double-checked, or
deferred to human expertise.
2. Related Works
Confidence estimation and calibration have a long history in
machine learning and natural language processing (Wang,
2024). With the rise of LLMs, a lot of attention has moved to
extracting and improving confidence estimation from these
new models. There is a wide range of methods that can
roughly be divided into black-box and white-box methods
(Geng et al., 2024).
Black-box methods require only the model generations for
uncertainty estimation and do not depend on any knowledge
of the model’s internal state. Within this group, linguistic confidence methods assess the uncertainty by simply
prompting the LLM to verbalize its confidence. Xiong
et al. (2024) showed that prompting techniques like chainof-thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022) can, to a limited extend, help the model in the calibration of its confidence
expression. Based on the assumption that uncertainty in
its generation would prime the model to hallucinate information, consistency-based methods (Manakul et al., 2023;
Wang et al., 2022) measure the similarity between multiple
generations and show that high variance in the generation
correlates with high uncertainty. Wang et al. (2022) propose
using CoT to produce various reasoning pathways towards
an answer. By marginalizing out the reasoning pathways,
they provide the most consistent answer as the one most
probably correct and offer the consistency measure as an estimation of the model’s confidence. Black-box methods are
valuable for their simplicity, ease-of-use and universality,
however generally lack behind white-box methods in their
calibration performance.

2. Related Works
Confidence estimation and calibration have a long history in
machine learning and natural language processing (Wang,
2024). With the rise of LLMs, a lot of attention has moved to
extracting and improving confidence estimation from these
new models. There is a wide range of methods that can
roughly be divided into black-box and white-box methods
(Geng et al., 2024).
Black-box methods require only the model generations for
uncertainty estimation and do not depend on any knowledge
of the model’s internal state. Within this group, linguistic confidence methods assess the uncertainty by simply
prompting the LLM to verbalize its confidence. Xiong
et al. (2024) showed that prompting techniques like chainof-thought (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022) can, to a limited extend, help the model in the calibration of its confidence
expression. Based on the assumption that uncertainty in
its generation would prime the model to hallucinate information, consistency-based methods (Manakul et al., 2023;
Wang et al., 2022) measure the similarity between multiple
generations and show that high variance in the generation
correlates with high uncertainty. Wang et al. (2022) propose
using CoT to produce various reasoning pathways towards
an answer. By marginalizing out the reasoning pathways,
they provide the most consistent answer as the one most
probably correct and offer the consistency measure as an estimation of the model’s confidence. Black-box methods are
valuable for their simplicity, ease-of-use and universality,
however generally lack behind white-box methods in their
calibration performance.
White-box methods, on the other hand, depend on access
to the internal state of the model, either for the evaluation
of logits and activations or for fine-tuning of the model for
calibration. Logit-based methods calibrate the confidence
by assessing the probabilities or the entropy of tokens in
the predicted sequence. Huang et al. (2023a) calculate the
mean probability of the generated tokens with the intuition
that a model that generates an answer with high probability
tokens also has a high confidence in this answer. Kuhn
et al. (2023) and (Duan et al., 2024) expand on this idea by
looking at the entropy of the generated tokens while also
taking the semantic relevance into account. Kadavath et al.
(2022) showed that LLMs can self-evaluate the correctness
of their own generation. They prompt the model to provide
an answer followed by a judgement whether its own answer
is "true" or "false". They then compare the probability of the
"true" or "false" token to calculate a confidence estimation.
While all the aforementioned methods are zero-shot methods, another line of white-box methods, proposes to train external models for confidence estimation. Xiong et al. (2024)
propose a method that trains a linear probe for assessing the
model’s confidence based on the activations of the LLM’s
hidden state. They evaluate the application of the probe to
various layers and train it with correctness labels of the task.
This approach does not explicitly train on the granularity of
confidence estimation and, therefore, is only indirectly able
to express a confidence gradient for fine-grained calibration.
Building on this approach, Mielke et al. (2022) give an LLM
access to the confidence extracted by the external probe and

Fine-tuning LLMs using Reinforcement Learning from human feedback (RLHF) has received increasing attention for
aligning the models with human preferences, avoiding toxicity or the generation of harmful content (Ouyang et al.,
2022; Lu et al., 2022). Outside of RLHF, RL has been
used to fine-tune LLMs for agentic interaction in textual
environments (Zhou et al., 2023; Carta et al., 2023).
Confidence estimation of LLMs using RL is a novel research
direction that, to the best of our knowledge, has only been
approached by Tao et al. (2024) and Xu et al. (2024). Tao
et al. (2024) build on the Reinforcement Learning with
Human Feedback (RLHF) paradigm and design a reward
function that aligns the verbalized confidence of the model
with the preference rating predicted by the RLHF reward
model. However, this approach can not evaluate model
confidence in factual statements and depends on humanannotated preference data. Xu et al. (2024) introduce a
novel Reinforcement Learning from Knowledge Feedback
(RLKF) framework, which aims to teach a model to refuse
to answer questions outside their knowledge scope, reducing
hallucinations. However, this does not quantify confidence
when giving an answer.
3. Rewarding Doubt
We propose a novel reinforcement-learning approach, that
improves an LLM’s ability to verbalize an accurate numerical confidence in a previously generated answer. The LLM
functions as an agent in a simulated environment as shown
in Figure 2, that poses challenging question-answering scenarios. It is prompted with task queries such as factual
questions and asked to predict both an answer to the query
as well as a confidence score. Based on the correctness of
the answer, and the expressed confidence, we reward the
model, incentivizing it to express a calibrated confidence.
Formally, let the model be provided with a textual question
or request q, prompting an answer-confidence pair (a, ˆp) as
response, where a is a textual answer with binary correctness value, and 0 ≤ˆp ≤1 is a numerical confidence score
representing the subjective probability the model assigns to
answer a being correct. We train this subjective probability
assessment to align with the true epistemic probability p∗,
which represents the actual likelihood of correctness given
the model’s internal knowledge state. If ˆp and p∗are aligned
the model is perfectly calibrated, meaning the probability
of correctness P(j(a) = 1) always equals the expressed
confidence:
P(j(a) = 1 | ˆp = x) = x,
∀x ∈[0, 1],
where j(·) is a correctness judging function that is 1 if
answer a is correct, and 0 otherwise.
The true epistemic probability p∗is not directly observable,
thus supervised learning of calibration is only possible by
constructing an artificial ground truth to approximate p∗.
Instead, we model this task as a Markov Decision Process
(MDP) defined by the tuple (S, A, T , R), where the model
learns to generate calibrated confidence scores through reinforcement learning. The MDP is defined by the following
components:
• State space (S): A state st ∈S consists of a natural
language question q, the model’s predicted answer a,
and the partial sequence of confidence tokens predicted
so far, if any. That is, st = (q, a, c1:t−1), where c1:t−1
represents the previously generated confidence score
tokens.
• Action space (A): The action space consists of selecting the next token ct in the confidence estimation
process from the LLM vocabulary, including numerical
tokens (e.g., representing percentages or probability

values) and a special end-of-sequence token that finalizes the prediction.
• Transition function (T (st+1 | st, at)): The environment transitions deterministically based on the language model’s autoregressive token generation process.
Given a state st = (q, a, c1:t−1) and an action ct, the
next state is defined as st+1 = (q, a, c1:t), i.e., the
sequence of confidence tokens is augmented by ct.
• Reward function (R): The reward is designed to reflect
the risk-reward tradeoff in betting. It is calculated based
on the correctness of the answer and the confidence assigned. Correct answers with high confidence are rewarded highly, but also penalized when incorrect.
With our reward design, the model learns to align its
expressed confidence with the true epistemic probability.
This not only improves the trustworthiness of LLMs in
collaborative human-AI scenarios but also helps users better
assess when AI tools should be trusted, double-checked, or
deferred to human expertise.
4. Experimental Setup
We conduct experiments comparing our approach to
black-box and white-box baselines, using the setup described
in Figure 3. The model is trained on a dataset consisting
of factual questions paired with correct answers and confidence levels, as well as incorrect answers with varying confidence levels. The
model is tested on a held-out test set consisting of factual questions paired with correct answers and confidence levels, as well as incorrect answers with varying confidence levels. The
model’s performance is evaluated using the Brier score and
the Expected Logarithmic Score (ELS), which are metrics
commonly used to evaluate the accuracy and calibration
of probabilistic predictions.
4.1. Dataset Construction
The dataset is constructed by prompting the LLM to
generate both an answer and a confidence score for a series
of factual questions. For each question, the LLM is
provided with a prompt that includes a correct answer and
a range of confidence scores. The LLM is then asked to
output both the answer and the confidence score. The correct
answer is provided, along with confidence levels ranging
from 0 to 1, incrementally. The model is trained on the
generated responses, with the goal of learning to associate
correct answers with high confidence and incorrect answers
with low confidence.
4.2. Model Architecture and Training
The model architecture follows the standard transformer
setup, with multi-head attention and feed-forward networks.
The model is fine-tuned using the AdamW optimizer with
weight decay, and learning rate set to 5e-4. The training
data consists of the input sequences (q, a, c1:t) and the
target confidence scores ˆp. The model is trained for 1000
iterations, with batch size 32. The validation loss is monitored
on a held-out validation set to prevent overfitting.
4.3. Evaluation Metrics
We evaluate the model’s performance using the Brier
score and the Expected Logarithmic Score (ELS). The Brier
score measures the mean squared difference between the
generated probability and the actual outcome. A lower Brier
score indicates better calibration. The Expected Logarithmic
Score (ELS) is the expected value of the logarithm of
the generated probability for correct answers and 1 minus
the logarithm for incorrect answers. A higher ELS indicates
better calibration.
4.4. Comparison Baselines
We compare our approach to several black-box and
white-box baselines, including:
• Black-box: The model is provided with the correct
answer and a confidence score, but no access to the
internal state or reasoning process.
• White-box: The model is provided with the correct
answer and a confidence score, and access to the internal
state for calibration purposes.
Additionally, we compare to the following approaches:
• Xiong et al. (2024): Consistency-based method for
calibrating confidence.
• Wang et al. (2022): CoT-based method for calibrating confidence.
• Kuhn et al. (2023): Logit-based method for calibrating confidence.
• Duan et al. (2024): Entropy-based method for calibrating confidence.
• Mielke et al. (2022): External probe for calibrating confidence.
• Tao et al. (2024): RLHF-based approach for calibrating confidence.
• Xu et al. (2024): RLKF-based approach for calibrating confidence.
5. Results
We present our experimental results comparing our
approach to several state-of-the-art methods, showing that
our method achieves better calibration scores on the test
set. Our results indicate that the model learns to express
calibrated confidence across a range of factual questions,
improving both the accuracy and the calibration of the
generated confidence scores. We analyze the calibration
scores across different confidence thresholds and demonstrate
that our approach achieves better performance compared to
the baseline methods.
